questions.q: Which statement best characterizes primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)?
ch: Pituitary disease with a low ACTH that spares aldosterone and causes no hyperpigmentation
Hypothalamic disease with a low ACTH in which the renin-aldosterone axis is fully preserved
Excess cortisol production by an adrenal cortical adenoma with a suppressed plasma ACTH level
Isolated aldosterone deficiency with a normal cortisol and a normal response to cosyntropin
Destruction of the adrenal cortex with deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone and a high ACTH
questions.exp: Primary adrenal insufficiency is destruction of the adrenal cortex, so both cortisol and aldosterone are deficient; the pituitary responds with a high ACTH, which drives hyperpigmentation.
why: Low ACTH with preserved aldosterone and no hyperpigmentation describes secondary insufficiency.
Hypothalamic (tertiary) disease also lowers ACTH and spares the renin-aldosterone axis.
Addison's disease is cortisol deficiency, not the cortisol excess of an adrenal adenoma.
Both cortisol and aldosterone are lost in primary disease, and the cosyntropin response is subnormal.

questions.q: In developed countries, what is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency?
ch: Abrupt withdrawal of chronic exogenous glucocorticoid therapy after long use
Tuberculous destruction of the adrenal glands, which remains a major cause worldwide
Autoimmune adrenalitis, often part of an autoimmune polyglandular syndrome
Adrenal hemorrhage from meningococcemia (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome)
Bilateral adrenal metastases seeded from a distant primary malignancy
questions.exp: Autoimmune adrenalitis is the most common cause of Addison's in developed countries and is often part of the autoimmune polyglandular syndromes.
why: Abrupt steroid withdrawal produces secondary insufficiency, not destruction of the adrenal cortex.
Tuberculosis is a major cause worldwide but not the leading cause in developed countries.
Adrenal hemorrhage from meningococcemia causes acute primary failure but is uncommon.
Adrenal metastases are sought on the etiology imaging workup but are not the usual cause.

questions.q: Which set of laboratory findings is classic for primary adrenal insufficiency?
ch: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and a mild metabolic acidosis
Normal sodium and potassium with an isolated elevated bicarbonate
Hypernatremia, hyperkalemia, and a marked metabolic alkalosis
Hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and a metabolic alkalosis
Hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and a respiratory alkalosis
questions.exp: Loss of aldosterone causes salt wasting with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and a mild metabolic acidosis; hypoglycemia and eosinophilia may also be present.
why: Electrolytes are characteristically deranged in primary disease rather than normal.
Sodium is low from salt wasting, and the acid-base disturbance is a mild acidosis.
High sodium with low potassium and alkalosis is the opposite pattern of mineralocorticoid excess.
Potassium is high, not low, because aldosterone deficiency impairs potassium excretion.

questions.q: A patient with fatigue, weight loss, and salt craving has hyperpigmentation of the skin creases, scars, and buccal mucosa. What does this finding indicate?
ch: Secondary insufficiency arising from pituitary disease with a low ACTH
Primary insufficiency, because a high ACTH and POMC-derived MSH drive pigmentation
Tertiary insufficiency arising from hypothalamic disease with a low ACTH
Adrenal insufficiency caused by chronic exogenous glucocorticoid therapy
Aldosterone deficiency alone, occurring independently of the ACTH level
questions.exp: Hyperpigmentation occurs only in primary disease: the failing adrenal cortex drives ACTH up, and POMC-derived MSH activity pigments skin creases, scars, and buccal mucosa.
why: Secondary disease lowers ACTH, so hyperpigmentation is absent — its absence points to secondary.
Hypothalamic (tertiary) disease also has a low ACTH and therefore no hyperpigmentation.
Chronic exogenous steroids suppress the HPA axis and ACTH, so pigmentation does not develop.
Pigmentation tracks the high ACTH and MSH of primary disease, not the aldosterone level.

questions.q: A low morning (8 AM) serum cortisol has been drawn. Which test confirms the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency?
ch: A 21-hydroxylase antibody titer sent with the initial screening labs
Adrenal CT imaging to look for hemorrhage, tuberculosis, or metastases
The ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test, looking for an inadequate cortisol rise
A single random afternoon serum cortisol repeated on a separate day
Plasma renin and aldosterone levels drawn while the patient is upright
questions.exp: A low morning cortisol is the screening test; the ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test confirms the diagnosis when the cortisol rise is inadequate.
why: 21-hydroxylase antibodies establish an autoimmune etiology after the diagnosis is made.
Adrenal CT belongs to the etiology workup, not to confirming the hormone deficiency.
A random afternoon cortisol is unreliable; screening uses a morning level and cosyntropin confirms.
Renin and aldosterone help localize primary disease but do not confirm cortisol deficiency.

questions.q: Why is fludrocortisone required in primary adrenal insufficiency but not in secondary insufficiency?
ch: Patients with secondary insufficiency have a high ACTH that maintains aldosterone output
Secondary insufficiency spares aldosterone, so mineralocorticoid replacement is unnecessary
Fludrocortisone is a glucocorticoid and hydrocortisone already supplies that activity
Secondary insufficiency causes more sodium wasting, which fludrocortisone would worsen
Fludrocortisone is used only during adrenal crisis, when stress dosing is inadequate
questions.exp: Fludrocortisone replaces aldosterone in primary insufficiency to retain sodium and excrete potassium; secondary insufficiency spares the renin-aldosterone axis, so it is not required.
why: Secondary insufficiency is defined by a low ACTH, and ACTH is not what drives aldosterone.
Fludrocortisone is the mineralocorticoid; hydrocortisone is the glucocorticoid replacement.
Salt wasting is a feature of primary disease, and salt should not be restricted.
In crisis, stress-dose hydrocortisone already supplies enough mineralocorticoid effect.

questions.q: A patient in adrenal crisis is hypotensive and vomiting. What is the nursing priority?
ch: Encourage oral rehydration and reassess the blood pressure in one hour
Sit the patient upright and obtain orthostatic blood pressures before treating
Obtain a morning cortisol and withhold treatment until the result returns
Restrict sodium and fluids to prevent overly rapid correction of the sodium
Obtain large-bore IV access, give rapid normal saline, and give IV hydrocortisone
questions.exp: The priority in crisis is circulation: large-bore IV access, rapid normal saline, and the prescribed IV hydrocortisone, while monitoring for shock.
why: Oral rehydration cannot reverse hypovolemic shock, and this patient is vomiting.
Orthostatic measurement is routine assessment, and abrupt position changes risk syncope.
Treat first and test later — waiting for results during a crisis can be fatal.
Aggressive normal saline is required, and salt is not restricted in primary insufficiency.

questions.q: A known Addison's patient with influenza who has missed several hydrocortisone doses arrives with a blood pressure of 76/44, vomiting, and confusion. What is the immediate management?
ch: Fludrocortisone alone, since aldosterone deficiency is causing the hypotension
A vasopressor infusion while awaiting the cosyntropin stimulation result
A potassium binder and insulin-dextrose for hyperkalemia before any steroid
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus with aggressive normal saline and dextrose
Oral hydrocortisone at double the usual dose together with oral fluids
questions.exp: Adrenal crisis is treated immediately with an IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus plus aggressive normal saline with dextrose, and by treating the precipitating illness — do not wait for test results.
why: Fludrocortisone is maintenance therapy; stress-dose hydrocortisone covers mineralocorticoid needs.
Steroids and saline come before confirmatory testing in a suspected adrenal crisis.
Hyperkalemia resolves with hydrocortisone and volume resuscitation, which must not be delayed.
The patient is vomiting and in shock, so oral dosing cannot be absorbed or relied on.

questions.q: You suspect adrenal crisis in an undiagnosed patient but still want to run a cosyntropin stimulation test. Which steroid should you give?
ch: Dexamethasone, because it does not interfere with the cortisol assay
Hydrocortisone, because its short half-life will not affect the cortisol assay
Fludrocortisone, because it has essentially no glucocorticoid activity at all
Prednisone, because oral dosing avoids interference with the cortisol assay
No steroid at all until the cosyntropin stimulation test has been completed
questions.exp: Dexamethasone is the crisis steroid of choice when the diagnosis is unconfirmed: it treats the patient without interfering with the cortisol assay, so cosyntropin stimulation can still proceed.
why: Hydrocortisone is measured by the cortisol assay and would invalidate the test.
Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid and does not treat glucocorticoid deficiency in crisis.
Oral therapy is inappropriate in crisis, and prednisone does not solve the assay problem.
Withholding steroids in a suspected crisis can be fatal — treat first, test later.

questions.q: A patient on lifelong hydrocortisone replacement develops fever and vomiting at home. What should the sick-day teaching have told them to do?
ch: Continue the usual dose and call the clinic in the morning if not improved
Take extra fludrocortisone and add dietary salt instead of the glucocorticoid
Skip the dose until the vomiting stops in order to avoid gastric irritation
Inject the emergency hydrocortisone and seek care, because vomiting blocks oral dosing
Halve the oral dose until the fever resolves, then resume the usual regimen
questions.exp: Sick-day rules: double or triple the oral dose with fever, and if vomiting, inject the emergency hydrocortisone and seek care. Steroids are never skipped or stopped.
why: Fever calls for an increased dose and vomiting calls for injection, not watchful waiting.
Extra mineralocorticoid does not replace the glucocorticoid needed for the stress response.
Steroids must never be skipped or stopped — omission precipitates adrenal crisis.
The dose must be increased for illness and stress, never reduced.

questions.q: Which sequence best describes the pathophysiology of infective endocarditis?
ch: Bacteria invade wholly normal endothelium and destroy the valve without any thrombus
Immune complexes deposit on the valve leaflets and later become secondarily infected
Chronic pressure overload thickens and calcifies the valve, which then becomes infected
Septic emboli lodge in the coronary arteries and seed the valve from the myocardium
Endothelial injury forms sterile platelet-fibrin thrombi that transient bacteremia then seeds
questions.exp: Endothelial injury creates sterile platelet-fibrin thrombi (nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis); transient bacteremia seeds these, forming infected vegetations that destroy valves and shed septic emboli.
why: A damaged or turbulent endothelial surface and a platelet-fibrin thrombus must come first.
Immunologic phenomena such as Osler nodes and Roth spots are consequences, not the initial lesion.
Structural heart disease is a risk factor because it creates turbulence and endothelial injury.
Septic emboli are shed from an established vegetation; they do not create it.

questions.q: Which organism is the most common overall cause of infective endocarditis, including right-sided disease in injection drug use?
ch: Staphylococcus aureus, the typical organism of acute virulent disease
Staphylococcus epidermidis, seen in early prosthetic valve infection
HACEK organisms, fastidious colonizers of the oropharynx
Viridans group streptococci from poor dentition or a dental procedure
Enterococcus faecalis arising from a genitourinary or GI source
questions.exp: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause overall and the organism of acute, virulent disease, including right-sided tricuspid endocarditis in injection drug use.
why: S. epidermidis is typical of early prosthetic valve endocarditis, not the leading overall cause.
HACEK organisms arise from the oropharynx and are an uncommon, fastidious cause.
Viridans streptococci cause indolent subacute disease linked to the mouth and dental procedures.
Enterococci are associated with a GU or GI source and are not the most common organism.

questions.q: Which peripheral finding of infective endocarditis is painful?
ch: Janeway lesions on the palms and soles
Splinter hemorrhages beneath the fingernails
Roth spots seen on retinal examination
Osler nodes on the finger and toe pulps
Petechiae on the conjunctiva and mucosa
questions.exp: Osler is Ouchy: painful nodes on the finger and toe pulps, an immunologic phenomenon. Janeway lesions, by contrast, are painless.
why: Janeway lesions are painless macules on the palms and soles caused by septic emboli.
Splinter hemorrhages are painless linear marks under the nails.
Roth spots are painless retinal lesions found on fundoscopy.
Petechiae are painless and are among the classic peripheral signs.

questions.q: By the Modified Duke (2023 ISCVID) criteria, which combination establishes definite infective endocarditis?
ch: 1 major criterion alone, with no minor criteria required
2 major criteria, such as sustained bacteremia plus echo evidence
1 major criterion plus 1 minor criterion in a predisposed patient
3 minor criteria alone in a patient with a fever above 38 degrees
2 minor criteria plus one positive blood culture from a single site
questions.exp: Definite infective endocarditis requires 2 major criteria, or 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria.
why: A single major criterion by itself is not sufficient for a definite diagnosis.
One major criterion requires three minor criteria, not one.
Five minor criteria are needed when no major criterion is met.
This reaches none of the accepted combinations; one culture is microbiologic evidence not meeting major.

questions.q: What is the nurse's responsibility regarding blood cultures in suspected infective endocarditis?
ch: Draw a single set from the existing central line after the first antibiotic dose
Draw cultures only when the temperature is above 38 degrees at that moment
Delay the cultures until echocardiography has confirmed a valve vegetation
Draw at least three sets from separate venipuncture sites before antibiotics
Draw two sets from the same site thirty minutes apart once vancomycin is running
questions.exp: At least three sets of blood cultures should be drawn from separate venipuncture sites using strict aseptic technique before antibiotics are started.
why: Cultures must precede antibiotics and must come from multiple separate venipuncture sites.
Fever is often intermittent, so cultures are not withheld for a normal temperature.
Cultures and echocardiography are the two pillars, and the cultures come first.
Separate sites are required, and drawing after vancomycin has started lowers the yield.

questions.q: Transthoracic echocardiography is negative in a patient with a prosthetic aortic valve and persistent Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. What is the next step?
ch: Repeat the transthoracic study in one week once antibiotics have taken effect
Obtain a transesophageal echocardiogram, essential for prosthetic valves and abscess
Proceed directly to surgical valve replacement without any further imaging
Order coronary angiography to look for a mycotic aneurysm of a coronary artery
Accept the negative study and treat this as bacteremia without endocarditis
questions.exp: Transesophageal echocardiography has higher sensitivity than TTE and is essential for prosthetic valves, small vegetations, and perivalvular abscess, so a negative TTE does not exclude endocarditis.
why: Delaying imaging risks missing a perivalvular abscess or progressive valve destruction.
Surgical timing is a multidisciplinary decision and still requires diagnostic imaging.
Angiography does not image vegetations; cardiac CT or PET are the advanced adjuncts.
A negative TTE does not exclude endocarditis with a prosthetic valve and sustained bacteremia.

questions.q: Blood cultures in an older patient with subacute endocarditis grow Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis). What should you order?
ch: Serology for Coxiella, Bartonella, and Brucella as fastidious organisms
Chest CT to look for septic pulmonary emboli from a tricuspid vegetation
Colonoscopy, because gallolyticus bacteremia is associated with colon cancer
Panoramic dental radiographs to look for a periapical or periodontal abscess
Urinalysis and prostate examination to identify a genitourinary portal of entry
questions.exp: Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) bacteremia should prompt a colonoscopy to look for colon cancer — always match the organism to its portal of entry.
why: Coxiella, Bartonella, and Brucella are considered in culture-negative disease; these cultures grew.
Septic pulmonary emboli suggest right-sided disease from injection drug use with S. aureus.
A dental source points to viridans group streptococci rather than gallolyticus.
A GU or GI source suggests enterococcus rather than gallolyticus.

questions.q: A patient who injects drugs has fever, a tricuspid regurgitant murmur, and multiple peripheral nodular opacities on chest imaging. Which statement best fits this presentation?
ch: Left-sided viridans streptococcal endocarditis seeded from poor dentition
Early prosthetic valve endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis
Enterococcal endocarditis arising from a genitourinary portal of entry
Culture-negative endocarditis caused by Coxiella or Bartonella species
Right-sided S. aureus endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli, often managed medically
questions.exp: Injection drug use causes right-sided tricuspid endocarditis with S. aureus and septic pulmonary emboli; right-sided disease is often managed medically, while left-sided disease is more embolic and dangerous.
why: Viridans streptococci come from the mouth and cause left-sided subacute disease.
Early prosthetic valve infection requires a prosthetic valve, which this patient does not have.
Enterococcal disease arises from a GU or GI source and does not shed septic pulmonary emboli.
Culture-negative disease follows prior antibiotics or fastidious organisms, not this classic picture.

questions.q: A patient being treated for aortic valve endocarditis develops new first-degree AV block that progresses on telemetry. What does this suggest?
ch: A perivalvular root abscess that requires urgent surgical evaluation
An embolic stroke involving the brainstem and its conduction pathways
Anemia of chronic disease producing a rate-related conduction delay
Immunologic glomerulonephritis with hyperkalemia slowing conduction
An expected effect of the beta-lactam antibiotic on the cardiac conduction system
questions.exp: New AV block or conduction delay on the ECG suggests a perivalvular or root abscess and is a red flag requiring urgent surgical evaluation.
why: Embolic stroke produces sudden focal neurologic deficits rather than progressive AV block.
Anemia is a laboratory finding in endocarditis and does not cause conduction block.
Hematuria and immunologic phenomena occur, but conduction block points to an abscess.
Nafcillin and cefazolin are linked to interstitial nephritis and neutropenia, not heart block.

questions.q: Which regimen is now favored for Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis in order to avoid aminoglycoside toxicity?
ch: Ampicillin plus gentamicin for a synergistic bactericidal effect
Penicillin G alone, dosed once daily as outpatient parenteral therapy
Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone as a double beta-lactam regimen
Rifampin plus nafcillin to penetrate biofilm on the infected valve
Vancomycin monotherapy given for a four to six week intravenous course
questions.exp: Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone is now preferred for Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis because this double beta-lactam regimen spares the nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity of gentamicin.
why: Ampicillin with gentamicin is the older regimen, and gentamicin is nephrotoxic and ototoxic.
Penicillin G or ceftriaxone alone is used for viridans streptococcal native-valve disease.
Rifampin is an adjunct for prosthetic valve staph infection and is never used as monotherapy.
Vancomycin is empiric coverage for staph, not the preferred definitive enterococcal therapy.

questions.q: Which description best fits the chest pain of acute pericarditis?
ch: Burning epigastric pain after meals that is worse when supine at night
A dull constant ache unchanged by position, breathing, or exertion
Crushing substernal pressure on exertion, relieved by rest and nitroglycerin
Sharp retrosternal pain that is worse lying flat and relieved by sitting forward
Tearing interscapular pain that is of maximal intensity at the moment of onset
questions.exp: Pericarditis causes sharp retrosternal pain that is pleuritic and positional — worse lying flat and with inspiration, relieved by sitting forward — and it may radiate to the trapezius ridge.
why: Postprandial burning that is worse supine suggests reflux rather than pericardial inflammation.
Pericardial pain is characteristically positional and pleuritic, not unchanged by position.
Exertional pressure relieved by rest describes angina, not pleuritic positional pain.
Tearing pain of instant maximal intensity suggests aortic dissection instead.

questions.q: Which ECG pattern is the signature of acute pericarditis?
ch: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, plus PR elevation in aVR
Deep symmetric T-wave inversion confined to the anterior precordial leads
Electrical alternans with low voltage across all twelve of the leads
Left bundle branch block with discordant ST changes in the lateral leads
Regional ST elevation with reciprocal ST depression in the opposite leads
questions.exp: Diffuse concave (upsloping) ST elevation with PR depression is the ECG signature of acute pericarditis, and PR elevation in aVR is a helpful clue.
why: Isolated anterior T-wave inversion is not the described pericarditis pattern.
Electrical alternans suggests a large effusion or tamponade rather than pericarditis itself.
Bundle branch block is not among the suggestive ECG changes for pericarditis.
Regional elevation with reciprocal depression describes STEMI; pericarditis is diffuse.

questions.q: How is the pericardial friction rub best heard?
ch: At the apex in the left lateral decubitus position using the bell
Over the right second intercostal space during a held inspiration
At the left sternal border with the patient leaning forward at end-expiration
At the posterior lung bases, where it persists unchanged over several days
Only with the patient lying completely flat and breathing quietly
questions.exp: The scratchy, triphasic rub is best heard at the left sternal border with the patient leaning forward at end-expiration; it is evanescent, so listen often.
why: The left lateral decubitus position with the bell is used for a mitral diastolic murmur.
The right second intercostal space is the aortic area, not where the rub is sought.
The rub is a pericardial sound at the left sternal border and it comes and goes.
Lying flat is the position that worsens the pain; the rub is sought leaning forward.

questions.q: How many of the four diagnostic criteria are required to diagnose acute pericarditis?
ch: 1 criterion: pleuritic positional chest pain by itself is sufficient
2 of the 4: pain, friction rub, ECG changes, or a new effusion
3 of the 4, one of which must be a documented pericardial effusion
4 of the 4, since every criterion must be documented before treating
0 criteria; the diagnosis rests entirely on excluding coronary syndrome
questions.exp: Diagnosis requires at least 2 of 4 criteria: pleuritic/positional chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, suggestive ECG changes, or a new or worsening pericardial effusion.
why: Chest pain alone is one criterion, and a second criterion is required.
Three criteria exceed the requirement, and an effusion is not mandatory.
All four are not required — many patients never develop a pericardial effusion.
Pericarditis has explicit positive criteria rather than being purely a diagnosis of exclusion.

questions.q: What is the evidence-based first-line drug therapy for acute idiopathic pericarditis?
ch: Opioid analgesia with activity restriction and watchful observation
Prednisone at a low-to-moderate dose with a slow and careful taper
Colchicine alone, dosed by weight and adjusted for renal impairment
An NSAID or aspirin combined with colchicine and gastroprotection
Anakinra or rilonacept to block interleukin-1 from the outset
questions.exp: An NSAID (or aspirin) plus colchicine is the evidence-based first-line combination, given with gastroprotection; colchicine speeds remission and halves recurrence.
why: Analgesia alone does not treat the inflammation or reduce the risk of recurrence.
Early corticosteroids raise the risk of recurrence and are second-line therapy.
Colchicine is added to an NSAID rather than used by itself as initial therapy.
Anti-IL-1 biologics are reserved for colchicine-resistant, steroid-dependent recurrent disease.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of adding colchicine, as shown in the ICAP and CORP trials?
ch: It prevents the troponin elevation that defines myopericarditis
It allows corticosteroids to be started earlier and at a higher dose
It removes the need to follow serial CRP during the medication taper
It resolves an existing pericardial effusion faster than drainage does
It roughly halves the risk of recurrent pericarditis and speeds remission
questions.exp: Colchicine added to an NSAID speeds remission and cuts recurrence roughly in half in the ICAP and CORP trials, and it is the mainstay of recurrent disease.
why: Troponin elevation reflects myopericarditis and is not what colchicine addresses.
Early steroids are specifically avoided because they raise the recurrence risk.
Serial CRP still guides the duration of therapy and the timing of the taper.
Pericardiocentesis, not colchicine, drains a large or tamponading pericardial effusion.

questions.q: Which feature most reliably distinguishes acute pericarditis from STEMI on the ECG?
ch: Diffuse non-territorial elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal depression
Sinus tachycardia accompanying the ST-segment changes on the tracing
T-wave inversion occurring at the same time as the ST elevation
The absolute height of the ST elevation measured in the inferior leads
The presence of pathologic Q waves within the first hour of symptoms
questions.exp: Pericarditis produces diffuse, non-territorial concave ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal ST depression except in aVR and V1; STEMI is regional with reciprocal depression.
why: Tachycardia is nonspecific and occurs in both conditions.
T-wave timing is not the discriminating feature; PR depression and no reciprocal change are.
The height of the elevation does not separate the two; distribution and the PR segment do.
Q waves are not part of the described distinction between pericarditis and STEMI.

questions.q: A patient with pericarditis becomes hypotensive with jugular venous distention, muffled heart sounds, and a pulsus paradoxus of 18 mmHg. What is required?
ch: Give a fluid bolus and repeat the ECG in two hours before intervening
Emergency pericardiocentesis to drain the effusion causing tamponade
Begin anakinra for colchicine-resistant, steroid-dependent recurrent disease
Increase the NSAID dose and add a proton pump inhibitor for gastroprotection
Start high-dose prednisone with a slow taper for refractory inflammation
questions.exp: Beck triad — hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart sounds — with a pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg indicates cardiac tamponade, an emergency requiring drainage by pericardiocentesis.
why: Tamponade is an emergency, and delaying drainage to repeat testing risks arrest.
Anti-IL-1 biologics treat recurrent disease, not acute hemodynamic compromise.
Escalating anti-inflammatory therapy does not relieve hemodynamic compromise from tamponade.
Corticosteroids are second-line anti-inflammatory therapy and do not treat tamponade.

questions.q: A patient with typical pericarditis has a rising troponin but a preserved ejection fraction on echocardiography. How is this best classified and managed?
ch: Dressler syndrome, treated with aspirin rather than with indomethacin
Effusive-constrictive disease requiring urgent pericardiocentesis today
STEMI requiring immediate cardiac catheterization and urgent reperfusion
Constrictive pericarditis requiring evaluation for surgical pericardiectomy
Myopericarditis — manage as pericarditis, restrict activity, monitor LV function
questions.exp: A troponin elevation with a preserved ejection fraction defines myopericarditis: manage as pericarditis but restrict activity and monitor left ventricular function. Elevated troponin is also a high-risk feature favoring admission.
why: Dressler syndrome is immune-mediated pericarditis weeks after an MI, which is not described.
Effusive-constrictive disease is a follow-up endpoint, and no tamponading effusion is described.
Pericarditis gives diffuse concave elevation without reciprocal change and is not reperfused.
Constriction presents later with Kussmaul sign, a pericardial knock, and right heart failure.

questions.q: Three weeks after a myocardial infarction a patient develops pleuritic positional chest pain and a friction rub. Which treatment is preferred?
ch: Ibuprofen, because non-aspirin NSAIDs are preferred after a myocardial infarction
Colchicine as monotherapy, without any additional anti-inflammatory agent
Aspirin combined with colchicine and gastroprotection
Indomethacin, chosen as the most potent NSAID for pericardial inflammation
High-dose prednisone started immediately in order to shorten the course
questions.exp: This is Dressler syndrome — immune-mediated pericarditis weeks after an MI. Aspirin is the preferred anti-inflammatory post-MI, combined with colchicine and gastroprotection.
why: Non-aspirin NSAIDs are avoided post-MI; aspirin is the preferred agent.
Colchicine is added to an anti-inflammatory rather than used alone as first-line.
Dressler syndrome is treated with aspirin, not with indomethacin.
Early corticosteroids raise the risk of recurrent pericarditis and are second-line.
